title: Munition Inventories: An Update Amid Renewed War Risk
gist: CSIS inventory update finds the US has enough munitions to renew war with Iran after expending a third to two-thirds of key stocks in the 39-day Operation Epic Fury, but missile-defense interceptors (Patriot, THAAD) are critically short for a China war; recovery takes 2-4 years and is constrained by time and production capacity rather than money, making multiyear FY2027+ funding the key variable.

themes.theme: Iran war drawdown: adequate for Iran, not China

insights.claim: In the 39-day campaign up to the April 8 ceasefire and subsequent operations, the United States expended between a third and two-thirds of key munition inventories, yet sufficient numbers remain for renewed conflict with Iran.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Renewed Iran strikes are feasible militarily, so munition constraints are not a brake on escalation risk in the Gulf.
insights.quote: the United States expended between a third and two-thirds of key munition inventories

insights.claim: The Department of Defense views every munition used against Iran as reducing capability and potentially deterrence against China, so the true measure of inventory adequacy is a China war.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Middle East expenditure directly erodes Indo-Pacific deterrence, raising Taiwan-scenario risk premia while stocks rebuild.

insights.claim: Most munitions take 2 to 4 years to be delivered after Congress appropriates funds, and timelines have lengthened because US and allied demand exceeds supply; the constraint is time, not money.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Defense-prime revenue visibility extends years out; the window of reduced US deterrence is multi-year regardless of budget.
insights.quote: The problem is not money, assuming Congress continues its support, but time.

themes.theme: Missile defense interceptors: the critical shortfall

insights.claim: Missile defense interceptors are in critical short supply, with prewar inventory already considered inadequate for a China war, and there are no substitutes because only specialized munitions can hit theater ballistic missiles exceeding 5,000 mph in terminal phase.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Interceptors are the scarcest, least substitutable category, making them the most durable demand driver in defense procurement.
insights.quote: Missile defense interceptors are in critical short supply

insights.claim: An estimated two-thirds of the prewar US Patriot interceptor inventory has been expended against Iranian ballistic missiles in the past nine months, with transfers to Ukraine further reducing stocks.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Extreme Patriot depletion underpins sustained orders for Lockheed Martin's PAC-3 line.
insights.quote: An estimated two-thirds of prewar Patriot interceptor inventory have been expended

insights.claim: Lockheed Martin targets annual Patriot interceptor production of 2,000, up from around 600 today (and about 300 per year before the Ukraine war), under a January 2026 framework agreement with the Trump administration, with a goal of 2,000 by 2030.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A >3x capacity ramp signals major multiyear revenue growth for Lockheed Martin's missile business.
insights.locator: Lockheed Martin has announced an annual

insights.claim: New Patriot interceptors face intense competition: 18 other countries operate Patriot, an estimated 1,600 interceptors were already in the allied backlog prewar, and in October the administration approved selling 500 interceptors to Ukraine, which reportedly ran out of Patriot stock.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Allied backlog ensures demand outstrips even expanded supply for years; allocation decisions become geopolitical levers.
insights.quote: Even before the war, an estimated 1,600 interceptors were in the allied backlog.
insights.locator: There will be a lot of

insights.claim: Around half of the prewar THAAD interceptor inventory is estimated to have been used in the Iran war, prompting DOD to resequence 2025-2026 deliveries to prioritize US stocks over Saudi Arabia and the UAE, while Lockheed plans to quadruple THAAD production capacity.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Gulf allies' THAAD deliveries slip; Lockheed capacity quadrupling is a further growth driver.

insights.claim: Ship-based Standard Missile interceptors were used less than ground-based ones, likely because destroyers stayed outside the Persian Gulf and can only reload in ports with specialized facilities, yet inventory recovery will still be slow due to small recent orders.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Naval interceptor stocks look healthier but remain fragile for a high-intensity Pacific fight.

insights.claim: SM-3 Block IIA costs $30 million versus $16 million for Block IB, offering 2,500 km versus 700 km range, while RTX seeks to increase SM-3 IIA production 2 to 4 times and grow SM-6 production to 500 per year.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: RTX is a primary beneficiary of naval interceptor ramp under the framework agreements.
insights.quote: RTX seeking to increase SM-3 IIA production “2 to 4 times” and grow SM-6 production to 500 per year

themes.theme: Cost asymmetry and the standoff-to-stand-in transition

insights.claim: US forces reached a 'point of munitions transition' by the fifth day of Operation Epic Fury, shifting from expensive standoff weapons to far cheaper short-range munitions of equivalent precision and payload; by day 14 less than 1 percent of US munitions fired were long-range.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: War cost is driven by the first days of exquisite munitions; a renewed campaign would likely transition faster and cost less.
insights.quote: less than 1 percent of munitions fired by U.S. forces were long-range

insights.claim: A JASSM and a JDAM-fitted BLU-110 both deliver 1,000-pound payloads accurately, but the JDAM has 15 miles of range at about $100,000 while the JASSM has 600 miles of range at $2.4 million.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Range is the main cost driver, so the munition mix (cheap vs exquisite) determines sustainable war spending.
insights.quote: The JDAM has a maximum range of 15 miles and costs about $100,000, while the JASSM has a range of 600 miles and costs $2.4 million.

insights.claim: The cheap stand-in transition achievable against Iran may not be achievable against China, because People's Liberation Army air defenses would take much longer to suppress and might keep short-range munitions from being used widely.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A China war would consume scarce long-range munitions for far longer, so Iran-war lessons understate China-war requirements.
insights.quote: it may not be achievable against a great power like China

insights.claim: Using AIM-120 AMRAAM ($1 million) and AIM-9X ($0.4 million) air-to-air missiles against Shahed drones costing an estimated $0.02 to $0.05 million each is impractical as a long-term option.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Cost-exchange imbalance drives demand for low-cost counter-drone interceptors from nontraditional suppliers.
insights.quote: Shahed drones are estimated to cost $0.02–0.05 million each

insights.claim: Low-cost counter-drone systems such as Roadrunner, Coyote and the Ukraine-tested Merops interceptor drone are being fielded, with several more in development, often from nontraditional suppliers with expertise in mass, low-cost manufacturing.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Counter-drone is an opening for new-entrant defense tech firms versus legacy primes.
insights.quote: often coming from nontraditional suppliers with expertise in technology, mass production, and low-cost manufacturing
insights.locator: Several other systems are in development

insights.claim: US destroyers and submarines have fired around a third of the prewar Tomahawk inventory in the Iran war; RTX plans to raise annual production to 1,000, but recovery will be slow because orders averaged only 86 missiles per year over the past 10 fiscal years.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Tomahawk production ramp of over 10x historical orders is a large incremental opportunity for RTX.
insights.quote: on average, 86 missiles per year in the past 10 fiscal years

insights.claim: Around a third of the prewar JASSM inventory was expended, but sizable procurement in prior years will rapidly restock it.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: JASSM is less of a bottleneck than interceptors or Tomahawk.

insights.claim: Operation Epic Fury was the first combat use of the Precision Strike Missile, whose low prewar stock will be quickly replenished by 964 Army missiles ordered between FY2024 and FY2026.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: PrSM inventories will grow sharply, expanding US land-based long-range fires.

insights.claim: Anti-ship munitions played little role against Iran but would be central against China; in CSIS wargames US players use bombers outside China's missile range firing long-range anti-ship missiles because close approach is suicidal early on.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Long-range anti-ship missile stocks are a key China-deterrence metric to watch in budgets.
insights.quote: China’s defenses make close approach suicidal
insights.locator: These munitions would play a major

insights.claim: Large bunker busters have limited inventory, and the reported option of using the MOAB against Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site may not fully damage the deeply buried facility.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Limits of conventional deep-strike leave Iran's nuclear program partially intact, sustaining escalation risk.

insights.claim: Ground munitions like Javelin were depleted mainly by transfers to Ukraine (about 40 percent of Javelin inventory) but are rebuilding, have not been used against Iran, and would probably not be used extensively in a US-China conflict.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Ground munitions are less of a strategic bottleneck than air-defense and long-range strike.

themes.theme: Why stocks are low and what fixes it

insights.claim: Low US munition inventories resulted from rational choices, not neglect: a post-Cold War strategy for short regional wars, an industrial base optimized for efficient peacetime production rather than surge, and services preferring visible platforms over munitions in budget fights.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Fixing shortages requires structural budget and industrial changes, not one-off supplementals.
insights.quote: the munitions industrial base was not neglected, nor were previous administrations blind to future needs

insights.claim: Of the 102 line items transferred to Ukraine, only Patriot has been used extensively in the Iran war, so Ukraine transfers were the main cause of ground-munition depletion but not of the Iran-related shortfalls.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Undercuts the narrative that Ukraine aid caused US Iran-war shortages.

insights.claim: DOD cannot afford adequate inventories using only exquisite, expensive munitions and needs a mix spanning a range of capabilities and costs.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Favors procurement of mid-tier and low-cost munitions and the firms producing them.

insights.claim: Industry's nightmare is that DOD deeply cuts munitions procurement when the crises ease, leaving unused capacity, so multiyear commitments in FY2027 and beyond are needed to induce private investment.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Multiyear procurement contracts are the key signal for defense-industry capex and earnings durability; watch FY2027 appropriations.

insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Munitions lines are likely protected even if topline defense spending disappoints.
